title: Cross-Entropy
body:
Simplification of [[KL Divergence]] which drops the $\log P(x)$ term 
[[Cross-Entropy Loss]]

---

Evan's first line is exactly right, and it is worth seeing why:

$$
D_{KL}(P\|Q) = \sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}
= \underbrace{\sum_x P(x)\log P(x)}_{-H(P)} - \underbrace{\sum_x P(x)\log Q(x)}_{-H(P,Q)}
$$

Drop the first sum and negate, and what is left is the cross-entropy:

$$
H(P,Q) = -\sum_x P(x)\log Q(x), \qquad H(P,Q) = H(P) + D_{KL}(P\|Q)
$$

**Read it as a cost.** You believe $Q$, so you build a code that spends $-\log Q(x)$ bits on
outcome $x$. Reality draws from $P$. Your average bill is $H(P,Q)$. If $Q = P$ this is
[[Shannon Entropy]] $H(P)$, the best achievable; otherwise it is strictly worse, and
[[KL Divergence]] is exactly how much worse.

Three properties to keep straight:

- **$H(P,Q) \ge H(P)$, always.** You cannot beat the true distribution's own code by using a wrong
  one. Equality only when $Q = P$.
- **It is not symmetric.** $H(P,Q) \ne H(Q,P)$, and the roles are not interchangeable: $P$ is
  truth, and it is what the expectation is taken over; $Q$ is your model, and it is what gets the
  logarithm. Swapping them is a different quantity with a different meaning.
- **$Q(x) = 0$ where $P(x) > 0$ makes it infinite.** Assigning zero probability to something that
  then happens is an unbounded error, which is why implementations clamp probabilities away from
  zero.

## Why it is the loss and not KL

$H(P) $ depends only on the data, not on the model's [[Weights]], so it is a constant during
training. **Minimising $H(P,Q)$ and minimising $D_{KL}(P\|Q)$ are therefore the same optimisation**,
and cross-entropy is the cheaper one to compute because that constant never has to be evaluated.
[[Cross-Entropy Loss]] is this quantity applied per training example.
